2.q: Bolt, Dot, Pim and Gizmo know their worlds. What can none of them do?
2.why: The four friends know their own worlds, but none of them can code. Coding the games is your job.

2.q: How many pieces does the Spark have?
2.why: The Spark is broken into four pieces, one for each world you will visit.

2.q: What must you score on the check to open the mission?
2.why: Two out of three opens the mission. The check makes sure the ideas landed before you play.

1b.why: The story says the Spark went dim, and coding the games is how it comes back.

choices: You do, by coding the games
Dot does, with her magnifying glass
1b.why: Bolt, Dot, Pim and Gizmo need a coder. That coder is you.

1b.q: What do you do in each step of the course?
choices: Read the story, pass the check, then play the mission
1b.why: Every step works the same way: story first, then the check, then the mission game.

2.q: What do you do with a program that almost works?
choices: Debug it: find and fix the mistake
2.why: A program that almost works is worth keeping. Debugging finds the one mistake and fixes it, instead of starting over.

choices: A whole message sent at once
A small piece of a message, sent across the network
2.why: A packet is one small, numbered piece of a message. The pieces travel across the network and are rebuilt at the other end.

2.q: What do coders do when a problem is too big to hold at once?
2.why: Decomposing splits a big problem into smaller parts you can solve and test one at a time.

1b.q: How many pieces of the Spark did you light?
1b.why: The Spark had four pieces, one for each world: Robo Route, Data Detective, Packet Post and Inside the Machine. You lit all four.

1b.q: Who coded the games that lit the Spark?
1b.why: Bolt, Dot, Pim and Gizmo know their worlds, but none of them can code. Every game that lit the Spark was coded by you.

choices: Build your own game in the Builder
1b.why: Coders do not only play games, they build them. The Builder is ready for your own game.

2.q: An app was tested only by Grade 5 bus riders. What is wrong with the test?
choices: It only asked one kind of user, so it can miss everyone else
Nothing: bus riders know apps best
The testers were the wrong age to test an app
One grade is always a big enough sample
2.why: A test is fair only when many kinds of users try the thing. One group cannot speak for everyone who will use it.

2.q: A reading app worked for 18 of 20 adults and 6 of 12 kids. Which comparison is fair?
choices: 18 worked and 6 worked, so adults win by 12
The app worked better for kids than for adults
Both groups did just as well
2.why: The groups are different sizes, so compare percents: 18 of 20 is 90%, and 6 of 12 is 50%. The app works far better for adults.

2.q: A lunch vote screen stood in the meat line, and burgers won the vote. The data is...
choices: Biased: the veggie eaters were never asked
Wrong: burgers never win a vote
2.why: The screen only reached one line, so a whole group never got a vote. People who are left out make data biased.
